lesson.title: Opening Doors with Cold War Rivals
lesson.summary: Even as he pursued a costly and unpopular ground war in Vietnam, President Nixon and his national security advisor Henry Kissinger pursued detente, a strategy of easing tensions with the Soviet Union and opening relations with communist China, reshaping Cold War diplomacy in the process.
lesson.body:
By 1970, Nixon faced a war that events like the shootings at Kent State had shown was tearing the country apart, alongside a decades long arms race with the Soviet Union that consumed enormous resources without making either side meaningfully safer. Rather than continuing to treat the communist world as a single, uniformly hostile bloc, as containment policy had generally done since the Vietnam War escalation of the 1960s, Nixon and Kissinger pursued a more flexible strategy known as detente, aimed at easing tensions through direct engagement rather than confrontation alone.

The most striking move was the opening to China. Nixon, who had built much of his early political career on staunch anti-communism, surprised the world by pursuing secret diplomatic contacts with the People's Republic of China, culminating in his personal visit to Beijing in February 1972, where he met with Chinese leader Mao Zedong. The opening exploited the deep rift between China and the Soviet Union, giving the United States new diplomatic leverage with both communist powers at once, and it also aimed to pressure North Vietnam by demonstrating that its major allies were willing to deal directly with Washington.

Nixon pursued a parallel opening with the Soviet Union, traveling to Moscow in May 1972 for a summit that produced the SALT I agreement limiting strategic nuclear weapons and a treaty restricting anti-ballistic missile systems, the first major agreements of the nuclear age aimed at slowing rather than winning the arms race. Alongside this diplomacy, Nixon pursued Vietnamization, gradually withdrawing American ground troops while shifting more of the fighting to South Vietnamese forces, a policy that eventually helped produce the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 and the withdrawal of remaining US combat forces from Vietnam.

Detente did not end the Cold War or the fighting in Vietnam, which continued between North and South Vietnamese forces until Saigon fell in April 1975, but it marked a significant shift in how the United States approached its adversaries, trading some of the rigid ideological confrontation of the earlier Cold War for pragmatic, if still wary, engagement. The diplomatic success also boosted Nixon's popularity heading into his landslide reelection in November 1972, the same year that a break-in at the Watergate complex, largely ignored by voters at the time, would set in motion the scandal that unraveled his presidency.
